summary: Defines two context headers for the Network Service Header (NSH), carrying subscriber and performance policy identifiers. Service functions in a service chain can use them to enforce policy and perform correct processing.

plainLanguage.summary: Tags attached to packets that tell the processing stations along the way who the traffic belongs to and what quality it should get.

questions: service function chaining policy context headers
what is the nsh subscriber identifier
what is the nsh performance policy identifier
subtitle: Two optional NSH context headers that tell service functions who the traffic belongs to and what performance policy applies.

tldr.problem: Service functions in a service chain sometimes need to know which subscriber a packet belongs to, or what performance treatment it needs, but the packet itself may not identify either unambiguously. For example, an inner IPv4 address is lost once a NAT has been crossed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two optional variable-length NSH context headers, Subscriber Identifier (type 0x00) and Performance Policy Identifier (type 0x01). Each carries an opaque value whose meaning is local to the SFC-enabled domain.
tldr.outcome: Service functions can enforce per-subscriber and per-service policy. The identifiers raise privacy questions, so the RFC recommends obfuscated, non-persistent values and stripping the NSH at the edge of the domain.

today: RFC 8979 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2021, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the NSH defined in RFC 8300.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Service Function Chaining architecture (RFC 7665) steers packets through a chain of service functions (SFs). Policy enforcement within a single administrative domain may need subscriber information, but the information carried in a packet may not be enough to identify a subscriber unambiguously. Traffic steering may also be driven by Quality of Service needs.

This RFC fills that gap with two new context headers for the Network Service Header (RFC 8300). They are carried in separate headers because subscriber identifiers differ from policy identifiers and several policies may apply to one subscriber. That avoids extra internal structure to say which kind an identifier is.

The RFC treats each identifier as an opaque value, and its semantics and validation are local policy. It covers only data plane behavior; control plane considerations are out of scope. The NSH is assumed to be used within a single administrative domain and is stripped at ingress and egress boundary nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers along a packet's trip sometimes need to know whose packet it is. These two labels carry that information without revealing it outside the building.

sections.title: Mobile Network Use Case
sections.content:
The RFC says the headers can apply to mobile networks, particularly the 3GPP-defined (S)Gi interface. Because private IPv4 addresses are widespread there, an SF located after a NAT function cannot identify a subscriber from the internal IPv4 address once the NAT has been crossed.

For a 4G network the NAT node can be the PDN Gateway (PGW), and for 5G it can be the User Plane Function (UPF). A mechanism to pass the internal information past the NAT boundary may optimize packet traversal, and some SFs not enabled on the PGW or UPF may need a subscriber identifier to operate. The RFC states that a comprehensive list of deployments is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a parcel goes through a re-labeling machine, the old return address is gone. A separate sticky note lets later stations still know whose parcel it is.

sections.title: The Subscriber Identifier Header
sections.content:
The Subscriber Identifier is an optional variable-length NSH context header. Its fields are Metadata Class (MUST be 0x0), Type (0x00), the U bit, Length (the identifier length in bytes) and the Subscriber Identifier itself, an opaque local identifier assigned to a subscriber by a network operator.

The RFC provides no cryptographic protection for the identifier, so any structure inside it is visible on the wire unless a secure transport encapsulation is used. Identifier values SHOULD be obfuscated. SFs use the header to enforce per-subscriber policies such as resource quota, customized filtering or accounting.

The classifier and NSH-aware SFs MAY inject the header according to local policy, and failures to inject should be logged locally. By default, intermediary nodes preserve the header, though local policy may have them strip it. NSH-aware SFs MUST ignore headers carrying unknown subscriber identifiers, and MUST ignore a header that fails local validation checks.

Several Subscriber Identifier headers MAY be present, each with a distinct opaque value for the same subscriber, for example when some SFs rely on IP addresses and others on non-IP identifiers. If an SF is told to strip the header, it MUST remove all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: This sticky note holds a secret code for the customer. Stations that do not know the code must ignore the note, and the code should be scrambled so nobody can guess who it is.

sections.title: The Performance Policy Identifier Header
sections.content:
The Performance Policy Identifier header differentiates services that need specific treatment, for example ultra-low latency (ULL) or ultra-high reliability (UHR). It lets downstream NSH-aware nodes pick suitable SFC paths, SF instances or SF policies. It is not helpful if path computation is centralized and a strict path is given to the SF Forwarders as local policy.

Its layout matches the subscriber header: Metadata Class (MUST be 0x0), Type 0x01, the U bit, Length, and an opaque identifier pointing to a performance policy whose structure and semantics are deployment specific.

Intermediate nodes preserve the header by default. Multiple headers MAY be present, each for a distinct policy. Conflicting policies complicate path computation, and when a node detects a conflict its default behavior is to discard the packet and send a notification alarm to a Control Element.
sections.plainLanguage: This sticky note says how the parcel must be treated, such as very fast or extra safe. If two notes disagree, the station stops the parcel and tells the boss.

sections.title: MTU and IANA
sections.content:
The extra NSH information makes packets bigger. Following RFC 8300, operators are RECOMMENDED to increase the underlying MTU so NSH traffic is forwarded within the domain without fragmentation. If they cannot, they may use a transport encapsulation with fragmentation handling, after carefully assessing the impact on SF Forwarders.

IANA assigned the two types from the NSH IETF-Assigned Optional Variable-Length Metadata Types subregistry (0x0000 IETF Base NSH MD Class): 0x00 for Subscriber Identifier and 0x01 for Performance Policy Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Sticky notes make the parcel a bit thicker, so the conveyor belt should be wide enough. The two note types also got official numbers so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Nodes in an SFC-enabled domain are assumed to be trusted, and the last SF Forwarder removes the NSH, so these identifiers do not leak outside the domain. Persistent identifiers facilitate tracking over time, so indirect and non-persistent identification is RECOMMENDED.

Multiple Subscriber Identifier headers let a misbehaving node inside the domain link them to one subscriber. Regularly randomized identifiers and removal by the last SF that uses them soften this. Without a secure transport encapsulation, trivial identifier structures such as IP addresses may reveal sensitive information to every on-path device. An SF keeping logs should not log header contents unless it uses them.

A misbehaving node could also alter the headers and disrupt service; the measures in RFC 8300 apply, and an integrity mechanism is described in an Internet-Draft. Notification alerts sent to a Control Element SHOULD be rate limited.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes stay inside the factory and are taken off at the exit. Inside, workers should only read them when they need to, and the codes should keep changing so nobody can follow one customer.
